title: Core Blockly Components
description: The five building blocks of every algorithm you'll write here: variables, loops, conditionals, arrays, and math operations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Every algorithm in this course is built from the same handful of core constructs, each shown as connectable, color-coded blocks.

subsections.title: What are Core Components?
subsections.content: Just like a mechanic has a standard toolkit, almost every program -- however complex -- is assembled from the same small set of building blocks.

subsections.title: The Five Pillars of Programming
subsections.content: Master these five and you can build almost anything:
bullets: **Variables:** your program's memory.
**Loops:** repetition.
**Conditionals:** decisions.
**Arrays:** organized collections of data.
**Math Operations:** calculations.

sections.title: Variables: The Program's Memory
sections.content: Variables hold information while your algorithm runs -- without them, a program can't remember anything.

subsections.title: Concept: Allocated Storage
subsections.content: Think of a variable as a labeled box in memory: give it a name, then read or overwrite what's inside whenever you like.

subsections.title: Common Data Types
subsections.content: A variable can hold:
bullets: **Numbers:** math and loop counters.
**Strings:** text.
**Booleans:** True or False.

subsections.title: Variable Operations
subsections.content: Three actions cover most of what you'll do:
bullets: **Create:** define a new variable with a name.
**Set:** give it a starting value.
**Change:** update it based on its current value (e.g. increment by 1).

subsections.title: Best Practices
subsections.content: Always set a variable before you try to change it -- modifying an unset variable throws a runtime error, since there's no baseline value yet.

sections.title: Loops: The Engines of Repetition
sections.content: A loop replaces a stack of repeated blocks with one reusable one -- keeping your algorithms compact and scalable.

subsections.title: Types of Loops
subsections.content: Three loop shapes, three use cases:
bullets: **Repeat (Counted):** runs a fixed number of times -- use when you know the count upfront.
**While (Conditional):** runs until a condition goes False -- use when the count is dynamic.
**For-Each (Iterative):** automatically visits every item in an array.

subsections.title: Micro-Transition: The Clock Analogy
subsections.content: Before nesting loops, get comfortable with a single one -- like a minute hand needing 60 full turns before the hour hand ticks once.

subsections.title: The Pointer Paradigm
subsections.content: Sometimes you need more control than For-Each gives you -- a While loop with your own tracking variables lets you walk an array from both ends at once, a key technique for optimized algorithms.

subsections.title: Common Pitfalls to Avoid
subsections.content: Watch your termination conditions:
bullets: **Infinite Loops:** a While condition that never goes False -- make sure something inside the loop actually updates it.
**Off-By-One Errors:** running one iteration too many or too few from a boundary mistake.

sections.title: Conditional Logic: Making Decisions
sections.content: Conditionals let your program branch -- checking its current state and picking the right path.

subsections.title: The Logic Toolbox
subsections.content: Decisions boil down to True/False evaluations, built from:
bullets: **Comparisons:** equality, greater/less-than.
**Boolean Operators:** AND, OR, NOT to combine conditions.

subsections.title: Structural Variants
subsections.content: Three shapes of branching:
bullets: **If:** runs only when true.
**If / Else:** one path or the other.
**If / Else-If / Else:** checks multiple conditions top to bottom.

subsections.title: Nested Conditionals
subsections.content: An If inside an If lets you check a sub-condition -- e.g. confirm admin status, then check a more specific permission.

sections.title: Arrays: Organizing Collections
sections.content: An array holds many related values in one ordered structure, instead of a separate variable for each one.

subsections.title: Zero-Based Indexing
subsections.content: Indexing starts at 0:
bullets: First item → index 0.
Second item → index 1.
Last item → length − 1.

subsections.title: Micro-Transition: Safe Array Reading
subsections.content: Practice *reading* from a list with a simple loop before you start modifying it -- small safe steps avoid crashes.

subsections.title: Array Operations
subsections.content: Core moves in the Arrays toolbox:
bullets: **Get / Set at Index:** read or overwrite a specific position.
**Append / Insert:** add an item at the end or at a specific index.
**Length:** count how many items are in the array.

subsections.title: Iterating Through Arrays
subsections.content: Arrays and loops go together naturally -- a For-Each loop over an array is the most common pattern you'll use.

sections.title: Math Operations: The Engine of Calculation
sections.content: Math blocks drive score-keeping, loop counters, and array boundary checks throughout your algorithms.

subsections.title: Available Math Blocks
subsections.content: Standard arithmetic plus Modulo, Exponents, rounding utilities, and random integer generation.

subsections.title: Order of Operations
subsections.content: Math blocks snap together horizontally and follow standard order of operations -- innermost block resolves first, working outward.

sections.title: Exploring Beyond the Core Components
sections.content: The five pillars are the foundation -- a few more toolbox categories round out what you can build.

subsections.title: Other Toolbox Categories
subsections.content: As activities need them:
bullets: **Input / Output:** print to console, prompt for input.
**Text / Strings:** concatenate, measure length, change case.
**Functions:** bundle instructions into a reusable custom block.

subsections.title: The Power of Experimentation
subsections.content: The fastest way to learn a new block:
bullets: **Direct Manipulation:** drop it on the canvas, feed it test values, run it, read the output.
**Python Observation:** watch the live Python panel to see exactly what it translates to.

sections.title: Lesson Summary
sections.content: Real algorithms combine these five pillars together. Here's what that looks like for finding the highest score in a classroom:

subsections.title: Combining Components
subsections.content: Step by step:
bullets: 1. **(Arrays)** Build a list of student scores.
2. **(Variables)** Create a "highest" variable, set to 0.
3. **(Loops)** For-Each over the scores.
4. **(Conditionals)** If the current score beats "highest"...
5. **(Variables)** ...update "highest" to the current score.
